In this section, we consider ciphers of class II and III (see Section 3.1) that cannot be fully described by polynomials over Ztpn . The attack strategy we follow is instead to find good polynomial approximations of the given cipher and exploit them. We quantify the quality of these approximations using the notion of polynomial correlation, PC, introduced in Section 5. The idea behind this attack strategy is not completely new in the literature. For example, in linear cryptanalysis [67], the goal of the attacker is to find the best linear approximation of a given cipher, in order to break it. A generalization is found in nonlinear cryptanalysis [58], in which the linear approximation is replaced by a low-degree approximation.

Since our algorithm requires a relatively high polynomial correlation to guarantee decoding, it is not suitable for approximating completely random or well-balanced functions. At the same time, the S-box of a given cipher may have been designed to appear random despite having a precise algebraic structure, as in the case of Streebog and Kuznyechik [68]. Our algorithm may allow for recovery of the original function in such cases. Interpolation Attack via Polynomial Approximation. A possibility to exploit a polynomial approximation of a cipher would be to set up an interpolation attack [54]. If the cipher admits a polynomial representation modulo pℓ for any ℓ ∈ {1, 2, . . . , n}, the attacker guesses the last round key(s), (partially) decrypts the given known ciphertexts, and constructs an interpolation polynomial modulo pℓ connecting the given plaintexts and the (partially) decrypted ciphertexts (the variable in the polynomial is the plaintext). Finally, an extra pair of plaintext/ciphertext is used to check if the guessed last round key is correct. Instead, if the cipher does not admit a polynomial representation modulo pℓ for any ℓ, and based on the considerations just given, it seems hard for the attacker to find a “sufficiently good” polynomial approximation for the (almost) entire cipher in an efficient way. Hence, we conjecture that the interpolation attack is in general not efficient in the case of a cipher of class II/III. 6.2 Solving the Associated System of Equations obtained via the Polynomial Approximation Rather than finding a good polynomial approximation for the entire cipher, the attacker can focus only on the non-polynomial parts of the cipher, that is, the 20

For example, the matrix multiplication M can be e.g. replaced with a function over a Galois Ring GR(pn , t) that provides diffusion. We leave the problem to study this case open for future work. 3.1 Choice of the Non-Linear Layer As recalled earlier, not every function over Zpn is a polyfunction. Due to this fact, several instantiations of a symmetric primitive are possible. Here, we list three possible cases, highlighting possible advantages and disadvantages based on the analysis proposed in the following. Class I: Polynomial S. As a first possibility, one may instantiate all the nonlinear functions S as polynomials. However, as already shown in [44, Section 2.2] (and recalled in Section 4), the corresponding symmetric primitive over Ztpn can be broken in time O(n·pt ) via a brute force attack. Roughly speaking, this means that pt must be sufficiently large in order to guarantee security, a condition that strongly depends on the considered application. In other words, if this condition is not satisfied, it is not possible to design a secure symmetric primitive over Ztpn instantiated with polyfunctions only. Class II: Non-Polynomial S. At the opposite end of the scale, one may ensure that none of the functions S admits a polynomial representation. One immediate consequence of this choice is that the algebraic attacks over Ftpn known in the literature would not work directly, as there is no immediate system of polynomial equations that succinctly describes the cipher. That said, the elements of Ztpn correspond one-to-one with the elements of Fpn (and Fnt t p ), and it is always possible to construct a polynomial representation over the latter. However, the arithmetics of these domains do not coincide for n ≥ 2, and we generally expect an algebraic representation over Ftpn to be dense and of high degree (for both linear and non-linear layers), making this attack approach infeasible.1
